question: A thin piece of wood of uniform density in the shape of an equilateral triangle with side length \(3\) inches weighs \(12\) ounces. A second piece of the same type of wood, with the same thickness, also in the shape of an equilateral triangle, has side length \(5\) inches. Which of the following is closest to the weight, in ounces, of the second piece?
solution:
Equal density and thickness mean that equal areas of the two pieces weigh the same, so their weights are proportional to their areas. Both triangles are equilateral, so their corresponding angles are equal and the triangles are similar.

The side-length scale factor is \(5/3\). Corresponding bases and heights both scale by this factor, so the area scales by its square. Therefore the second piece weighs
\[
12\left(\frac53\right)^2
=12\cdot\frac{25}{9}
=\frac{100}{3}\text{ ounces}.
\]
This is \(33\frac13\) ounces. It differs from \(33.3\) by only \(1/30\) ounce, while every other choice is more than \(13\) ounces away. The closest weight is \(33.3\) ounces, choice D.

edges.reason: The integer-multiplier case supplies a useful stepping stone and repeated-addition interpretation. The product-of-numerators/product-of-denominators rule follows directly from a part-of-a-part area model without executing the earlier decimal-free integer-multiplier procedure; Gemini confuses this customary progression with necessity.
Contexts such as price, quantity and total, or speed, time and distance, supply familiar examples. Direct proportion can be learned through other contexts like side length and perimeter.
Direct proportion rests on a constant ratio value, which is ratio meaning. Proportion equations matter only when problems are solved by setting up a proportion.

The criteria identify an invariant ratio and use its value to find the other quantity. This requires the quotient meaning of a ratio, without the additional cross-product property of proportions.
